title: The Learning Science of Deliberate Practice
author: Kognitivo
summary: Kognitivo argues that self-diagnoses like 'I'm just not a math person' are resignation letters disguised as facts about innate talent, and that the actual research-backed answer to the nature-versus-practice debate is deliberate practice, a specific and demanding form of training defined by K. A. Ericsson. The piece distinguishes naive practice (repetition that plateaus into autopilot), purposeful practice (structured, goal-directed, and feedback-driven), and deliberate practice proper, which additionally requires an established domain with objective standards and an expert coach who can target a learner's specific, self-invisible weaknesses. It debunks the popularized '10,000-hour rule' as a distortion of Ericsson's actual violin-student study, and cites a Swedish twin study to show genetics and environment still explain real variance in expertise beyond hours logged. The piece closes by noting that while talent and starting age are fixed, one variable remains fully within a learner's control: what they choose to do in their very next practice session.
points: Ericsson's three-tier practice hierarchy is the article's central framework: naive practice plateaus into autopilot, purposeful practice adds structure and feedback, and deliberate practice further requires an established domain with objective standards plus an expert coach targeting individualized weaknesses.

The popularized '10,000-hour rule' is directly debunked: Ericsson's actual number was an average among elite violinists specifically, many elite performers had far fewer hours, and Gladwell's bestseller never even engaged with the concept of deliberate practice itself.

A Swedish study of over 10,000 twins found that when one identical twin practiced music considerably longer than their co-twin, no difference emerged in basic musical abilities like pitch and rhythm discrimination, showing genetics still bounds outcomes.

The coach requirement in deliberate practice exists because 'the most dangerous errors are usually the ones you can't perceive yourself' — without outside correction, thousands of repetitions can simply build 'a very durable mistake.'
quotes: There's actually a best-supported answer researchers have found to the question "how do people become exceptional?". It's a specific and demanding way of practicing called deliberate practice.

The most dangerous errors are usually the ones you can't perceive yourself. If you've rehearsed a subtle mistake for a thousand hours, however structured your goals, you'll build nothing but a very durable mistake!
10,000 isn't a magical number, it's the average of the best group of violinists only. Many of the best violinists had far fewer hours and were already elite by the age of 20.

In the cases where an identical twin had practiced music for considerably longer than their co-twin, no difference could be found between them in their basic musical abilities (pitch and rhythm discrimination).

The honest answer to the talent-versus-practice question is that experts are made, out of the materials they were born with. No one gets to choose the raw materials, but everyone chooses what they do with them.
It looks like a diagnosis, but it's actually a resignation letter. And it's addressed to the only variable that you were ever in charge of.
